clinicalPearls: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome of symptoms and signs arising from any structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection; it is the common final pathway for most chronic cardiovascular diseases including hypertension, coronary artery disease, and valvular disease (p.1975).

Roughly half of patients with HF have reduced ejection fraction (EF less than or equal to 40%, HFrEF) and about half have preserved (greater than or equal to 50%, HFpEF) or mildly reduced (41-49%, HFmrEF) EF; because most patients have both systolic and diastolic abnormalities, the older terms 'systolic' and 'diastolic' heart failure have been abandoned (p.1977).

An EF that recovers to normal on guideline-directed therapy defines HF with recovered EF (HFrecEF); predictors include younger age, shorter HF duration, nonischemic etiology, smaller ventricular volumes, and absence of fibrosis, and withdrawal of therapy can cause symptom and EF recurrence in up to half of patients within 6 months (p.1977).

Dyspnea progresses in severity as exertional dyspnea, then orthopnea, then paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, then dyspnea at rest; bendopnea (breathlessness when bending forward) reflects elevated filling pressure, especially with low cardiac output (p.1982).

Orthopnea typically occurs within 1-2 minutes of lying down, whereas paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea occurs after prolonged recumbency and may require 30 minutes or more upright for relief; cardiac asthma (wheezing) can mimic primary lung disease (p.1982).

An S3 gallop indicates volume overload, suggests severe hemodynamic compromise, and carries negative prognostic significance, whereas an S4 is nonspecific and often reflects hypertensive HFpEF (p.1984).

Pulmonary rales may be ABSENT in longstanding HF despite chronically elevated wedge pressures because increased lymphatic drainage prevents alveolar spillage, so a clear chest does not exclude congestion (p.1983, p.1985).

Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP) rise with wall stress and aid diagnosis when uncertain, but levels are falsely LOW in obesity and falsely elevated by age, female sex, chronic kidney disease, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism, and pulmonary arterial hypertension (p.1985).

Cardiorenal syndrome is driven not only by reduced forward cardiac output but importantly by systemic and abdominal venous congestion; relieving congestion (diuretics or ultrafiltration) often improves renal function (p.1981).

High-output HF is rare and usually requires underlying structural heart disease; consider it with severe anemia (often hemoglobin less than or equal to 8 g/dL), arteriovenous fistula, severe obesity, cirrhosis, thyrotoxicosis, end-stage renal disease, or beriberi (p.1982).
Iron deficiency (with or without anemia) is common in chronic HF; IV iron (not oral) improves symptoms, exercise capacity, and reduces hospitalizations, though survival benefit is uncertain (p.1985).

Q waves with reduced QRS voltage (pseudo-infarct pattern) suggest infiltrative or restrictive cardiomyopathy such as amyloid, and conduction system disease should raise suspicion for cardiac sarcoid or Chagas in the right setting (p.1985).
harrison.pathophysiology: HFrEF is a progressive disease in which an index event (acute MI, chronic pressure/volume overload, genetic or congenital disease) triggers months to years of cardiovascular remodeling. Pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy and volume overload produces eccentric hypertrophy; both involve myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, altered calcium-handling and cytoskeletal proteins, reexpression of fetal genes, and myocyte necrosis, apoptosis, and autophagy, completing a vicious cycle of pump dysfunction and rising wall stress. Compensatory neurohormonal activation of the sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports output but becomes maladaptive, causing vasoconstriction, sodium and water retention, baroreceptor dysfunction, direct myocardial toxicity, arrhythmia, and adverse remodeling of heart, vessels, and kidneys. Counterregulatory vasodilators (ANP, BNP, prostaglandins, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, nitric oxide) are upregulated and act via guanylate cyclase to promote vasodilation and natriuresis; bradykinin and natriuretic peptides are degraded by neprilysin. Endothelin, inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, IL-6), and reactive oxygen species contribute to remodeling. HFpEF mechanisms are less defined but extend beyond diastolic dysfunction to vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, adiposity-related inflammation, oxidative/nitrosative stress, and insulin resistance. Electrical dyssynchrony (LBBB/IVCD), secondary mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, cardiorenal and splanchnic/hepatic congestion, gut microbiome alterations with endotoxemia, and high-output states further drive progression.
additionalDifferentials: HFpEF versus noncardiac causes of dyspnea and fluid retention (the diagnosis of HFpEF requires ruling these out)
Asthma or COPD (wheezing/rhonchi from bronchial congestion can mimic these)
Biliary tract disease (right HF hepatic congestion causes RUQ pain, nausea, abnormal liver tests)
Pneumonia and primary lung disease (chest x-ray helps distinguish)
Constrictive pericarditis or restrictive cardiomyopathy (Kussmaul's sign and massive ascites)
Cardiogenic versus noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (may require invasive hemodynamics)
infectionMimics: Viral, giant cell, or sarcoid myocarditis presenting with new HF
Sepsis as a precipitant or high-output contributor
nonInfectiousMimics: Pulmonary arterial hypertension and right HF
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive metabolic panel, CBC, coagulation studies, urinalysis; selected testing for diabetes, lipids, thyroid function
12-lead ECG (LVH, prior infarction, conduction disease, atrial fibrillation, QRS width/LBBB for resynchronization eligibility)
Chest x-ray (cardiothoracic ratio greater than 0.5, upper-zone venous redistribution, interlobular septal thickening, alveolar edema, pleural effusions)
Two-dimensional echocardiography with Doppler; speckle-tracking strain imaging for prognosis
Natriuretic peptides (BNP, NT-proBNP) for diagnosis, severity, and prognosis
Cardiac MRI for etiology and tissue characterization; cardiac CT/coronary CT angiography when MRI contraindicated; cardiac PET for ischemia/viability and sarcoid inflammation
Coronary angiography to exclude reversible ischemic cause
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (peak VO2, VE/VCO2 slope) for transplant/MCS evaluation and unexplained dyspnea
Invasive hemodynamics (pulmonary artery catheter; combined right/left heart catheterization to distinguish restriction from constriction)
Endomyocardial biopsy in selected cases (myocarditis, amyloidosis, chemotherapy/immunotherapy injury, transplant rejection)

Targeted etiologic screening: hemochromatosis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis; serum free light chains/SPEP, ferritin, ceruloplasmin, ANA, RF, hepatitis C, HIV; three-generation family history and genetic testing for inherited cardiomyopathy
redFlags: Acute pulmonary edema with severe dyspnea and pink frothy sputum (marked wedge pressure elevation)
Hypotension with narrow pulse pressure and rapid thready pulse, cool extremities, peripheral cyanosis (low-output/cardiogenic shock)
Kussmaul's sign (inspiratory rise in JVP) signaling severe biventricular HF and poor outcome
Oliguria from severely reduced renal blood flow (advanced-stage HF)
Marked elevation of transaminases and lactic acid suggesting cardiogenic shock
Cardiac cachexia (unintentional edema-free weight loss greater than 5% over 12 months) with muscle wasting and frailty
harrison.prognosis: Overall 5-year survival after HF diagnosis in primary care is about 50%, and 1-year mortality may reach 40% in severe HF. Post-admission mortality ranges from 8-14% at 30 days to 26-37% at 1 year and up to 75% at 5 years, with readmission of 20-25% at 60 days and nearly 50% at 6 months; risk of death rises with each subsequent admission. Most deaths are cardiovascular, from progressive HF or sudden cardiac death. Black patients have higher case-fatality, men higher age-adjusted mortality than women. Independent predictors of adverse outcome include older age, male sex, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, coronary disease, advanced NYHA class, S3 or elevated JVP, reduced LV/RV EF, elevated wedge pressure, low cardiac index and peak VO2, pulmonary hypertension, worsening renal function, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia, elevated troponin and natriuretic peptides, elevated neurohormones, widened QRS/LBBB, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular arrhythmias. HFrecEF carries a better prognosis than HFrEF or HFpEF. Overall outcomes are improving with risk-factor treatment and guideline-directed therapies.
pitfalls: Relying on signs and symptoms alone, which are neither sensitive nor specific for HF; maintain a high index of suspicion in high-risk patients (older, hypertension, diabetes, CKD).
Excluding HF because the lung exam is clear; rales can be absent in chronic HF with chronically elevated wedge pressures.
Misreading right-HF hepatic congestion (elevated transaminases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) as biliary tract disease.
Misdiagnosing cardiac asthma/bronchial congestion as primary asthma or COPD and treating inappropriately.
Over- or under-interpreting natriuretic peptides without accounting for obesity (falsely low) and for age, female sex, CKD, AF, PE, and PAH (falsely elevated).
Equating NYHA functional class with objective cardiac structure or function; it correlates poorly with EF and peak VO2.
Attributing diuretic-refractory nonpitting edema to HF when it represents lymphedema needing different workup.

Failing to seek precipitating factors (identifiable in 50-90% of admissions), such as nonadherence, excess salt/fluid, NSAIDs, negative inotropes, ischemia, arrhythmia, infection, anemia, thyroid disease, or sleep apnea.
harrison.severityClassification: New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification: Class I, no limitation, ordinary activity causes no undue symptoms; Class II, mild limitation, comfortable at rest but ordinary activity (e.g., carrying heavy packages) causes fatigue, dyspnea, palpitations, or angina; Class III, moderate limitation, comfortable at rest but less-than-ordinary activity (e.g., getting dressed) provokes symptoms; Class IV, severe, symptoms of HF or angina at rest, worsening with any activity. EF-based phenotypes: HFrEF (EF less than or equal to 40%), HFmrEF (41-49%), HFpEF (greater than or equal to 50%). The chapter notes NYHA class correlates poorly with objective measures such as LV size, EF, and peak oxygen consumption.
management: Confirm the diagnosis and classify by ejection fraction into HFrEF, HFmrEF, and HFpEF using echocardiography and natriuretic peptides to direct therapy

Initiate and up-titrate guideline-directed medical therapy in HFrEF with an angiotensin-receptor-neprilysin inhibitor or ACE inhibitor, a beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and an SGLT2 inhibitor
Relieve congestive symptoms with loop diuretics titrated to volume status
Identify and treat the underlying cause and precipitants including coronary ischaemia, valvular disease, atrial fibrillation, and hypertension
Offer device therapy with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator or cardiac resynchronisation where criteria are met
Monitor symptoms, weight, renal function and electrolytes, and serial natriuretic peptides through a specialist heart-failure service
Provide self-care education and vaccination, and escalate refractory disease to advanced therapies or palliative care

valueTables.title: NYHA and CCS functional classes
columns: New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class

cells.text: Cardiac disease without limitation of physical activity. Ordinary activity does not cause undue fatigue, palpitation, dyspnea or anginal pain.
Ordinary activity such as walking and climbing stairs does not cause angina. Angina occurs with strenuous, rapid or prolonged exertion at work or recreation.
Cardiac disease with slight limitation of physical activity. Comfortable at rest. Ordinary activity causes fatigue, palpitation, dyspnea or anginal pain.

Slight limitation of ordinary activity. Angina on walking or climbing stairs rapidly, walking uphill, walking or climbing stairs after meals, in cold, under emotional stress, or only in the few hours after awakening. Angina on walking more than two blocks on the level or climbing more than one flight of stairs at a normal pace in normal conditions.
Cardiac disease with marked limitation of physical activity. Comfortable at rest. Less than ordinary activity causes fatigue, palpitation, dyspnea or anginal pain.
Marked limitation of ordinary physical activity. Angina on walking one to two blocks on the level and climbing more than one flight of stairs in normal conditions.

Cardiac disease with inability to carry on any physical activity without discomfort. Symptoms of cardiac insufficiency or the anginal syndrome may be present even at rest. Any activity increases discomfort.
Inability to carry on any physical activity without discomfort. Anginal syndrome may be present at rest.
